passage: At the community centre, Kavitha stood at the door greeting the weekend class. Ayesha, five, put a hand on her chest and said, "Assalamu alaikum, Aunty." Behind her a boy pressed his palms together and said, "Namaste." Another child bowed his head shyly. Kavitha smiled at each, answering "Wa alaikum salaam" to Ayesha, "Namaste" to the boy, and a warm nod to the shy one. Ayesha whispered, "Everyone says hello different."

qa.q: What did Ayesha do with her hand when she greeted Kavitha?
qa.a: She put it on her chest.

qa.q: What might Ayesha be feeling as she whispers "Everyone says hello different"?
qa.a: Curious and perhaps pleased to have noticed it. She might also be a little unsure whether her way is the right one.

qa.q: How did Kavitha's replies help the children?
qa.a: She answered each child in their own form, showing that every greeting was respected.

qa.q: How might the shy child feel receiving just a nod?
qa.a: Comfortable, since no words were demanded. He might also wonder whether it counted as a proper greeting. 🙂

grounding: Shows young children greeting with salaam, namaste and a bow, each form respected and varying by family and faith.

passage: I'm Deepak, and this was at my mother's birthday. Little Mahima, five, came in with her grandparents, bent down and touched my mother's feet, then joined her palms. "Namaste, Dadi." My mother put a hand on Mahima's head. Mahima glanced back at her parents to check, and her father nodded. I couldn't tell if the look on her face was pride or relief.

qa.q: What did Deepak's mother do after Mahima touched her feet?
qa.a: She put a hand on Mahima's head.

qa.q: Why might Mahima have glanced back at her parents?
qa.a: To check she had done it right, which shows the greeting matters to her. She may also just have wanted their approval.

qa.q: How can adults teach a child ceremonial greetings kindly?
qa.a: Show the greeting, explain that families do it differently, and praise the effort.

qa.q: How might Deepak's mother feel about Mahima's greeting?
qa.a: Touched and welcomed, since she answered with a blessing.

grounding: Shows a preschooler greeting an elder with a namaste and feet-touching, seen by a host at a family gathering.

passage: At the church-run preschool, Joseph, five, folded his hands before lunch. "Thank you, God, for rice and dal. Amen." Anjali Ma'am smiled. "What are you saying thank you for?" "For food. And Amma made it. And the farmer." "That's a lot of people." "Is God the farmer's friend?" Anjali tilted her head. "What do you think?" Joseph thought hard. "I think yes."

qa.q: What did Joseph thank God for?
qa.a: Rice and dal.

qa.q: What might Joseph be feeling when he asks whether God is the farmer's friend?
qa.a: Curiosity and warmth as he tries to connect the people in his prayer. He may just be linking ideas in his head.

qa.q: How did Anjali support Joseph's question?
qa.a: She asked what he thinks instead of giving him a lecture.

qa.q: How might the other children see Joseph's prayer?
qa.a: As part of the lunch routine they share, which they may copy or simply wait through. 😊

grounding: Shows a preschooler saying thanks before a meal and asking a simple question about its meaning.

passage: I'm Kavitha, and I was on the train seat opposite Ayesha's family. Before eating, Ayesha, five, whispered "Bismillah" with her hands cupped, then smiled. "Ammi, what does Bismillah mean?" Her mother said, "In the name of God. We say it to be thankful before we eat." Ayesha nodded and started on her paratha. I can't know what she felt, but she looked calm.

qa.q: What word did Ayesha whisper before eating?
qa.a: "Bismillah."

qa.q: What might Ayesha be feeling when she asks what it means?
qa.a: Curiosity, wanting to understand a routine she already follows. She looked calm, so it may also just be a comfortable habit.

qa.q: How did Ayesha's mother respond to the question?
qa.a: She answered simply and warmly, giving the meaning in a few words.

qa.q: How does Kavitha see the moment?
qa.a: As a quiet outsider who respects it, and she admits she cannot know what Ayesha felt.

grounding: Shows a preschooler saying a short blessing before a meal and asking what it means, seen by a fellow traveller.

passage: In the hill village, Binita signed EAT to her son Tenzin, five, who is deaf, with her eyebrows raised. Tenzin signed YES and ran to the table. Later, Binita signed EAT again with a calm face and a small nod. Tenzin went straight to wash his hands. When her brows rose at a spilled cup, he looked at her whole face and saw surprise, not a question, and laughed.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do when Binita signed EAT with raised eyebrows?
qa.a: He signed YES and ran to the table.

qa.q: How did Tenzin read Binita's raised eyebrows the first time, and could they mean something else?
qa.a: He read them as a question. Raised brows can also show surprise, so he looks at her whole face and the situation.

qa.q: What could a hearing relative learn from this?
qa.a: To watch faces as well as hands, since facial movement is part of the grammar and not only emotion.

qa.q: How might Binita feel when Tenzin answers correctly?
qa.a: Pleased that they understand each other so easily. 😊

grounding: Shows a young child reading raised brows as a question in sign, where facial movement is grammar and not only emotion.

passage: At a family gathering in Bristol, Mina, five, who is deaf, watched her aunt Freya sign JUICE with eyebrows up and head tilted. Mina signed YES and ran to the fridge. Later Freya looked at a spilled glass, eyebrows up again, and signed JUICE with wide eyes and an open mouth. Mina laughed. That face meant "oh no!", not an offer. She signed, "Sorry, spilled."

qa.q: What did Mina do after her aunt's raised-eyebrow JUICE sign?
qa.a: She signed YES and ran to the fridge.

qa.q: What did Mina think Freya was feeling at the spilled glass?
qa.a: As surprise, "oh no", rather than an offer. She read the whole face, though she could have been wrong.

qa.q: What could a hearing newcomer learn from this?
qa.a: That facial movement is part of signed grammar, so the whole face should be watched along with the hands.

qa.q: How might Freya feel seeing Mina understand her?
qa.a: Proud and connected, since Mina read the difference at once.

grounding: Shows a young child reading raised brows and facial expression in sign, where the face is part of the grammar.

passage: Kunal, five, practised the new sign for "mango" at the dining table. He copied the handshape but signed it near his chest. His father Samir, who is deaf too, smiled and signed, "Same hand, wrong place. Try your cheek." Kunal moved his hand to his cheek and Samir nodded. "Chest is another word." Kunal signed it right twice, then signed "more mango" with a grin.

qa.q: Where did Samir tell Kunal to make the sign?
qa.a: At his cheek.

qa.q: How did Kunal probably feel when he signed it correctly?
qa.a: Pleased and proud, shown by his grin. He may also have been excited to ask for more mango.

qa.q: How could Samir keep teaching Kunal?
qa.a: Correct one feature at a time, place first, praise the try, and use real wants like mango to practise. 😊

qa.q: How might Samir see Kunal's early mistake?
qa.a: As a normal part of learning, like a hearing child saying a new word a little wrong.

grounding: Shows a young signer learning that handshape, location and movement together make a sign.

passage:
"Ball!" signed Yusuf, five, and pointed at the sofa.
"Where?" signed his cousin Abhinav, hands turned up.
"On!" Yusuf's hand hopped over the other.
Abhinav shook his head, smiling. "Under," he signed, sliding his hand beneath. "Same hands, different way."
Yusuf copied it slowly. "Under the sofa," he signed.
Abhinav gave a thumbs up and fetched the ball.

qa.q: Where was the ball, according to Yusuf's second try?
qa.a: Under the sofa.

qa.q: What might Yusuf feel when Abhinav shakes his head?
qa.a: Perhaps a flicker of doubt or embarrassment. Abhinav's smile shows it is friendly, and Yusuf tried again.

qa.q: How did Abhinav teach the sign?
qa.a: He showed the difference in movement and had Yusuf copy it slowly.

qa.q: How might Abhinav feel fetching the ball?
qa.a: Pleased he could help Yusuf learn, and glad the message got through.

grounding: Shows a young signer refining the movement of a sign, learned like the sounds of a spoken language.

subtype: Drawing and early writing of messages [Expressing]
passage: Note from Jomon, nursery teacher. Avni (5) gave me a card: a big yellow circle, a row of wavy lines she called "writing", and a stick figure with a huge smile. She read it aloud. "Dear Miss, thank you for the story, love Avni." I didn't correct the letters. I said, "Thank you, I love the smile." She grinned and asked me to hang it up, so it went beside the window. 🙂

qa.q: What did Avni call the wavy lines?
qa.a: Writing.

qa.q: What was Avni feeling when she gave Jomon the card?
qa.a: Affection and gratitude, shown by the smiling figure and the words she read out. She may also have wanted to please him.

qa.q: How should an adult respond to a card like this?
qa.a: To the meaning and the picture, not the spelling.

qa.q: How might Avni feel seeing the card hung by the window?
qa.a: Proud, since she asked for it to go up and it did.

grounding: Shows a preschooler drawing and scribbling a thank-you card, with an adult responding to the meaning rather than the spelling.

subtype: Drawing and early writing of messages [Expressing]
passage: On the courtyard step of the village house, Keerthana, six, scribbled wavy lines, a boat and a big red heart on the back of a calendar page. "It says, Papa, come home soon," she told her grandmother. They held it up to the phone camera. Her father Sahil, working in another town, leaned close to the screen. "I can read it. Come home soon. Thank you, beta. I'm counting the days."

qa.q: What did Keerthana say her message said?
qa.a: "Papa, come home soon."

qa.q: What might Keerthana feel about her father being away?
qa.a: She probably misses him, shown by the message and the big heart. She may also be excited to show him her work.

qa.q: How did Sahil respond to the drawing?
qa.a: He responded to the meaning, reading it out and thanking her, and did not comment on the spelling.

qa.q: How might Sahil feel seeing the message on the screen?
qa.a: Touched, and perhaps a little homesick.

grounding: Shows a preschooler drawing and scribbling a message of longing to a parent, met with warmth for the meaning.

subtype: Dramatic play and acting out roles [Expressing]
passage:
"Open wide," said Gopika, five, holding a toy stethoscope to her teddy. "This will hurt a tiny bit. Don't cry. Be brave."
"Doctor, is it going to be big?" squeaked her father Arnab in the teddy's voice.
"Small. And I hold your hand." She pressed a sticker on the teddy's arm. "Plaster."
"Papa, tomorrow the real doctor is for me."
"I know. Shall we practise once more?"
"Yes. But I have the plaster."

qa.q: What did Gopika press on the teddy's arm?
qa.a: A sticker, as a plaster.

qa.q: What might Gopika be worried about, given the game she is playing?
qa.a: Worry about the real doctor's visit tomorrow. Playing the doctor lets her feel in charge of it.

qa.q: How can Arnab support Gopika's play?
qa.a: Play along, answer her questions honestly and simply, and not hurry her out of the game. 🤍

qa.q: How might Arnab feel voicing the teddy?
qa.a: Gentle and attentive, since the play lets him hear her worry without pushing.

grounding: Shows a preschooler playing doctor with a teddy to work through worry about a real visit.

subtype: Dramatic play and acting out roles [Expressing]
passage: Note from Uday, teacher. During free play Harsha (5) roared as a monster and chased three children, who shrieked and ran happily. Then he stopped, hid behind the curtain and said in a small voice, "The monster is scared of the dark." I sat nearby. "What does the monster do when it's dark?" "He holds a torch." I gave him a paper torch. Nobody was hurt, and the play seemed to help him handle a worry. I'll watch how he is at nap time.

qa.q: What does the monster hold when it is dark?
qa.a: A torch.

qa.q: What might Harsha be feeling behind "The monster is scared of the dark"?
qa.a: Possibly worry about the dark himself, though it may just be part of the pretend story.

qa.q: How did Uday respond?
qa.a: He asked about the monster first and gave a paper torch, without treating the play as wrongdoing.

qa.q: How did the other children seem to see the chase?
qa.a: As fun, since they shrieked and ran happily.

grounding: Shows a preschooler acting a scary monster and revealing a worry, with a teacher treating it as play.

passage: Kunal, five, made a sock puppet rabbit talk on the sofa in the flat. "Rabbit is sad because his friend went away." Samir Uncle, at the other end of the sofa, sat lower. "Rabbit, what happened with your friend?" "He didn't share the swing. Rabbit stood alone." "That sounds lonely. What does Rabbit want?" "A friend who says, come play." Samir just nodded, and Kunal's rabbit hopped onto his lap.

qa.q: Why did Kunal say Rabbit was sad?
qa.a: Because his friend went away.

qa.q: What might Kunal be feeling as he talks through the rabbit?
qa.a: Perhaps lonely or left out, but we cannot be sure the story is about him. The puppet may simply be a safe way to say it.

qa.q: How did Samir handle the story wisely?
qa.a: He asked the rabbit questions and did not press Kunal to say it was about him.

qa.q: How might Kunal feel when Samir speaks to the rabbit?
qa.a: Heard and safe, which is why the rabbit keeps talking and hops onto his lap. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young child telling a puppet story with feelings and an adult asking about the character first.

passage:
Parul, six, held up a felt lion. "Lion is not going to the party."
"Why not?" said her father Harish, speaking to the lion.
"Because they'll laugh at his roar."
"That sounds hard for Lion. What does Lion want?"
"To roar loud and nobody laughs."
"Maybe Lion can practise with a friend." Parul made the lion nod. "Lion says okay. Papa, can you be the friend?"
"I'd love to."

qa.q: What is Lion not going to?
qa.a: The party.

qa.q: What might Parul be feeling as she tells Lion's worry?
qa.a: Perhaps worry about being laughed at herself, though we cannot be sure it is about her.

qa.q: How did Harish respond to the story?
qa.a: He spoke to the lion, asked what Lion wants and offered to practise, without saying the story was about Parul.

qa.q: How might Harish feel about being asked to be the friend?
qa.a: Warm and glad she is letting him in, and careful not to push.

grounding: Shows a child voicing a worry through a felt lion, with a father asking about the character first.

passage: Note from Gargi, teacher. Neelam (5) drew a house, a big yellow sun and four people in bright colours, the smallest one purple and smiling beside a dog. "Tell me about your picture." "That's Mama, that's Papa, that's me and Bruno." Mama was in black. I noticed, but did not read meaning into it. "What is Mama doing?" "Going to work in her black coat." Colour alone tells me little, so I will keep listening.

qa.q: What colour was Mama drawn in?
qa.a: Black.

qa.q: What might Neelam feel about her family, judging by her picture?
qa.a: Cheerful, since the picture has bright colours, a big sun and a smile. It is only a starting point, not proof.

qa.q: How did Gargi use the drawing?
qa.a: She asked Neelam to tell her about it and did not read meaning into the black colour.

qa.q: How might Neelam see the black she used for Mama?
qa.a: Simply as Mama's work coat, as she said.

grounding: Shows a preschooler drawing her house, sun and family, with an adult treating it as a start for conversation and not reading colour as a diagnosis.

passage: At the farm, Chaitanya, five, drew a house, a huge sun and four people on the back of a seed packet. Her grandfather Pradeep pointed. "That's you, that's Ma, that's Baba." "And the buffalo with big horns, bigger than the house." "Why is the buffalo so big?" "Because she gives milk." "And who is this small one in the corner?" "That's me. I'm drawing from here." Pradeep laughed and asked her to tell him about the sun.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya draw bigger than the house?
qa.a: The buffalo with big horns.

qa.q: What might the huge buffalo show about Chaitanya's feelings?
qa.a: That she values her, since she said "Because she gives milk". The size may also just be for fun.

qa.q: How should adults use a child's drawing like this?
qa.a: As a start to conversation, asking questions and not diagnosing from size or colour.

qa.q: How might Pradeep read the small figure in the corner?
qa.a: With curiosity but not worry, since Chaitanya explained she was drawing from there.

grounding: Shows a preschooler drawing a house, sun and family, with a grandfather asking questions and not over-interpreting.

passage: It was a rushed evening and Aparna had only a few minutes before her bus to the night shift. Rukmini, five, pressed a crumpled paper rakhi into her hand. "For you. You're my Mama." Aparna crouched, tied it round her wrist and said, "Thank you. I'll wear it at work." Rukmini beamed and waved from the window as the bus pulled away.

qa.q: What did Rukmini press into Aparna's hand?
qa.a: A crumpled paper rakhi.

qa.q: What might Rukmini feel when Aparna ties it on so quickly?
qa.a: Pleased and loved, since she beamed and waved. She may also have wished for a little more time together.

qa.q: How does a warm reception like this teach a child?
qa.a: It shows that feelings can be shared through objects, even when the response is quick. 🤍

qa.q: How might Aparna feel with only a few minutes?
qa.a: Rushed but touched, since she stopped to crouch and tie it on.

grounding: Shows a preschooler pressing a handmade rakhi into a parent's hand to show affection, received warmly despite time pressure.

passage: After dinner in the flat, Shreya, five, pressed a folded drawing into her mother's hand. "For you. Because you made rotis even when you were tired." Manjula unfolded it: two smiling stick figures and a sun with a face. "Thank you, Shreya. I like the sun's smile." She stuck it on the almirah door. Shreya watched it go up, then ran off to draw another for Papa.

qa.q: Where did Manjula stick the drawing?
qa.a: On the almirah door.

qa.q: Why might Shreya have watched the drawing go up?
qa.a: She wants to see her gift valued, and to feel her thanks was received. She may also simply enjoy seeing it displayed.

qa.q: What did Manjula's response teach Shreya?
qa.a: That feelings can be shared through objects, and that a warm welcome encourages more.

qa.q: How might Manjula feel opening the drawing?
qa.a: Touched, and perhaps tired from the day. She smiled and put it where she would see it.

grounding: Shows a preschooler giving a drawing to say thank you, received warmly.

passage: On Monday, Jahnavi, five, wore a red towel as a cape and flew around the flat. On Wednesday she buttoned her father Rafiq's shirt over her clothes, held a spoon like a thermometer and announced, "I'm the doctor." On Saturday she tied a dupatta as a saree and told her teddies to sit for lessons. "What will you be when you grow up?" Rafiq asked. "Today I'm the teacher!" she said, and went to fetch chalk.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi use as a cape on Monday?
qa.a: A red towel.

qa.q: What might Jahnavi feel when she says "Today I'm the teacher!"?
qa.a: Playful excitement. She enjoys trying roles on, and she is not deciding her future.

qa.q: How could Rafiq support Jahnavi's play?
qa.a: Join in, ask about the roles, and not treat any of them as fixed. 😊

qa.q: How might Rafiq see the different costumes?
qa.a: As play rather than a career plan, since he asked about the future and she answered about today.

grounding: Shows a preschooler trying on different roles through costumes as imaginative play that does not fix identity.

passage: On fancy-dress morning they overslept, and there was almost no time. Pallavi found an old yellow raincoat and a paper hat. "Firefighter!" said Himani, five. On the way it began to pour, and Himani pulled up the hood. "Firefighters aren't scared of rain!" At school she saw a friend dressed as a queen. "Tomorrow I'm a queen," she told her mother.

qa.q: What did Himani wear as her firefighter costume?
qa.a: An old yellow raincoat with a paper hat.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when she announced she would be a queen tomorrow?
qa.a: Curiosity and excitement about trying another role. She may also have felt a little envious of the queen costume.

qa.q: How could Pallavi respond to the new plan?
qa.a: Smile and play along, and perhaps let her dress up as a queen at home another day.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel after the rushed morning?
qa.a: Stressed at first, then relieved and amused that the raincoat worked.

grounding: Shows a preschooler wearing a firefighter costume and already wanting to try a queen, illustrating dress-up as imaginative play.
